home.page_title: Will the voltage on this street be safe?

overview.eyebrow: Day-ahead guard for streets with rooftop solar
overview.lede: At midday, rooftop solar pushes power back into the street and raises the voltage, which damages appliances and trips inverters. GridTwin forecasts when that will happen, tests every fix in a physics simulation, and tells a planner how much more solar the street can take.

overview.plain_hours: Under {rule}, the street is likely to be unsafe for about {hours} hours.
overview.plain_solar: Most of it is rooftop solar pushing the voltage up around midday.
overview.plain_grid: Most of it is the grid's own voltage: the street stays unsafe even with every panel switched off.
overview.plain_fix: The best fix the physics confirms: {fix}.
overview.plain_nofix: No fix that was tried makes the whole day safe; the closest is {fix}.

player.how: Press play to watch the day, quarter hour by quarter hour. Moving current on a wire is power: amber flows back towards the transformer when a home's panels make more than it uses (reverse flow); blue flows to the homes when they draw from the grid. Thicker and faster means more power. A house's roof shows its voltage, and it pulses when it is outside the rule. Tap a house for its numbers. On the timeline, bars above the line are power drawn and below it power sent back; red marks the quarter hours that break the rule ({steps} on this day).
player.flow_note: Voltages, solar, losses and the transformer come from the full power-flow calculation. Each home's solar is the street's solar times its share of the panels (the model has one sky for the street); its demand and net power come from the flows on its own wire, accurate to about a tenth of a kilowatt. The homes are grouped by the phase they are connected to and ordered by how far along the wire they are; on the real street the three phases run together on the same poles.
charts.sim_intro: Press play or drag the timeline. The map and both charts move through the same simulated day.
charts.voltage_intro: The highest and lowest home voltage at every quarter hour; dashed lines are the safe limits.
charts.voltage_label: Highest and lowest street voltage through the day, current time {time}
charts.why_title: Why it happens: solar versus home use
charts.why_intro: When solar rises above what homes use, the extra power flows back through the wires and pushes voltage up.
charts.why_label: Solar production and home electricity use through the day, current time {time}
proof.flow_estimate: The moving wire flows on the street picture are an estimate: each wire carries the net power of the homes beyond it. They leave out wire and transformer losses, a community battery's charging and discharging, the extra reduction of Volt/Watt, and reactive power, including the inverters' Volt/VAR. The voltages, loadings and every safety verdict come from the full power-flow calculation, not from this estimate.
overview.fact_sun: At midday, rooftop panels send power back into the street's wires, and the voltage at the far homes rises above the safe limit.
overview.fact_act: From tomorrow's weather forecast it simulates many versions of the day and shows when the voltage is likely to break the rule.
overview.fact_ok: Every fix is tested in the same simulation. If none keeps the whole day safe, GridTwin says so and names what stops it.
overview.journey_intro: Start with the forecast, then find a fix, plan for more solar, test the future, and check how far to trust it.

fixguide.tap.name: Transformer tap
fixguide.tap.what: A switch inside the transformer that lowers the voltage it sends to the whole street by a small step.
fixguide.tap.how: Midday voltage starts lower, so solar has more room before it reaches the limit.
fixguide.tap.who: The utility's lineman, with the transformer switched off for a few minutes; usually set once a season.
fixguide.tap.tradeoff: Almost free, but it also lowers the evening voltage, so homes far away can drop too low after sunset.
fixguide.inverter.name: Smart inverters
fixguide.inverter.what: A setting in each solar inverter that reacts to high voltage by itself, using the standard curves of the national inverter standard.
fixguide.inverter.how: Volt/VAR makes the inverter absorb reactive power, which pulls the voltage down; Volt/Watt reduces solar output only while the voltage is high.
fixguide.inverter.who: The solar installer or the home owner changes a setting; no new hardware on new inverters.
fixguide.inverter.tradeoff: Cheap; Volt/VAR adds a little wire loss, Volt/Watt loses some solar energy at the worst moments.
fixguide.combined.name: Combination
fixguide.combined.what: Two or more fixes used together, usually the transformer tap with smart inverters.
fixguide.combined.how: The tap lowers the whole street; the inverters handle the remaining peaks where they happen.
fixguide.combined.who: The utility sets the tap; installers set the inverters.
fixguide.combined.tradeoff: More coordination, but each part is cheap and the result is often the first safe option.
fixguide.curtailment.name: Export cap
fixguide.curtailment.what: Every home may send only part of its solar back to the grid.
fixguide.curtailment.how: Less power flows back up the wire, so the voltage rises less.
fixguide.curtailment.who: A setting in each inverter, required by the utility.
fixguide.curtailment.tradeoff: Simple but blunt: every home loses solar energy, even where the street had room.
fixguide.envelope.name: Per-home export limits
fixguide.envelope.what: A limit for each home and each quarter hour of tomorrow, sent the evening before.
fixguide.envelope.how: Only the homes and hours that cause the problem are limited; everyone else exports freely.
fixguide.envelope.who: The utility computes the limits; connected inverters follow them.
fixguide.envelope.tradeoff: Loses far less solar than a flat cap, but needs inverters that can receive a schedule.
fixguide.phase.name: Re-balance phases
fixguide.phase.what: Some homes are reconnected from a busy phase to a quieter one.
fixguide.phase.how: Solar and demand are spread evenly over A, B and C, so no single phase rises far, and the neutral carries less current.
fixguide.phase.who: A lineman moves the home's service wire at the pole; the plan says exactly which homes.
fixguide.phase.tradeoff: A visit per home moved, once; no lasting cost.
fixguide.battery.name: Community battery
fixguide.battery.what: A shared battery at the point of the street with the worst voltage.
fixguide.battery.how: It charges from the midday solar surplus and gives the energy back in the evening.
fixguide.battery.who: The utility or a community buys, installs and runs it.
fixguide.battery.tradeoff: The most expensive option; it also adds evening supply.
fixguide.switching.name: Feeder switching
fixguide.switching.what: A normally open switch between two feeders is closed and another opened, so part of the street is fed a different way.
fixguide.switching.how: Homes at the far end get a shorter path to the transformer, so their voltage rises less.
fixguide.switching.who: The utility operates the switches; the street stays radial.
fixguide.switching.tradeoff: Needs a tie switch to exist; a few switching operations.

proof.page_title: How far can you trust it?
proof.page_intro: Every check is run by a script and its result is kept, including the ones that failed. Here they are, grouped by the question they answer.
proof.score_line: A failed check is shown, not hidden: it tells you where not to rely on GridTwin yet.
proof.q_physics_intro: The voltages come from a power-flow calculation; these checks compare it with an independent tool and test it on unequal phases.
proof.q_forecast_intro: Tomorrow's sunshine and demand drive everything else.
proof.q_risk_intro: When GridTwin says a quarter hour is likely unsafe, is it right more often than a simple average would be?
proof.g.G1: The engine matches an independent power-flow tool
proof.g.G1_why: The same street and day are solved by GridTwin and by pandapower; the voltages must agree and GridTwin must be much faster.
proof.g.G2_why: Tomorrow's sunshine comes from several weather models; each must deliver almost every hour.
proof.g.G3: The solar forecast beats the first model
proof.g.G3_why: On the same days, the new solar forecast must make smaller errors than the first one.
proof.g.G4: The demand forecast beats simple rules
proof.g.G4_why: Household demand must be predicted clearly better than "same as yesterday and last week", with honest ranges.
proof.g.G5_why: With homes on single phases, the calculation must converge, and the result must stay stable under different assumptions.
proof.g.G6_why: Meter data and street data are open; the free weather service is for non-commercial use only.
proof.g.G7: Solar yield checked against a real plant
proof.g.G7_why: Needs measured data from a real plant, which is behind a login; until then the standard loss assumption is used.
proof.g.G8_why: Past days are replayed and the chances are compared with what really happened, on both districts.
explain.title: What the labels mean
explain.intro: Every colour and tag on this page, in plain words.
explain.ok_text: No quarter hour of the day reaches even the watch level. Nothing to do.
explain.watch_text: In at least one quarter hour, one in five or more of the simulated days is unsafe. Keep an eye on it.
explain.act_text: In at least one quarter hour, more than half of the simulated days are unsafe. Plan a fix for tomorrow.
explain.solar_text: The part of the risk that disappears when every panel is switched off in the simulation.
explain.grid_text: The part that stays even with every panel off: the voltage arriving at the transformer is already too high or too low.
explain.v_ok_text: The home's voltage is comfortably inside the rule.
explain.v_near_text: Inside the rule but within a few volts of its edge.
explain.v_over_text: Above the rule's upper limit: appliances can be damaged and inverters switch off.
explain.v_under_text: Below the rule's lower limit: fans and pumps struggle.
explain.ph_abc_text: Three live conductors. Each home is connected to one of them, so the three can carry very different loads.
explain.ph_n_text: The return conductor. It carries the difference between the phases: zero when they are equal, large when one phase is much busier.
explain.ph_flow_text: Power on a conductor. Towards the homes when they draw from the grid, back to the transformer when solar exports. Faster and thicker means more power.
explain.observed_text: Measured: real smart meters or real records.
explain.modeled_text: Calculated by GridTwin's forecasts and simulation.
explain.benchmark_text: From the standard test street, not a surveyed street of a real utility.
explain.p10p90_text: The range most simulated days fall inside: one in ten is lower, one in ten is higher.
explain.design_day_text: The sunniest of the day's simulated versions; fixes and the street replay are checked against it.
explain.safe_text: With this fix, no quarter hour of the day breaks the rule in any tested case.
explain.unsafe_fix_text: The fix helps, but some quarter hours still break the rule.
explain.recommended_text: The cheapest safe fix: least solar lost, fewest operations, then the most margin.
explain.no_safe_text: Nothing that was tried keeps the whole day safe. GridTwin shows the closest option and what it would still need.
explain.binding_text: The limit that is broken first: too high a voltage, too low a voltage, or an overloaded wire or transformer.
explain.approve_text: The new system adds no unsafe quarter hour.
explain.conditions_text: Safe only with a condition, such as an export limit or a smart-inverter setting.
explain.refuse_text: Unsafe even with the conditions tried; GridTwin gives the largest size that would pass.
explain.headroom_text: Extra kW of solar that can be added at a place and phase without making any quarter hour worse.
explain.pass_text: The check met the bar that was written down before it was run.
explain.fail_text: It did not; the true number is shown and no claim is made beyond it.
explain.conditional_text: Fine for this demo and research, with a condition for real use.
explain.not_run_text: The data needed for the check is not accessible yet.
explain.before_after_text: The same day without and with your changes, so the difference is only what you changed.
explain.better_worse_text: Green means the street moved away from its limits; red means closer to them.

player.home_nosolve: Home {home} on phase {phase}: no result for this quarter hour
player.nosolve_note: At this quarter hour the power flow has no solution for part of the street: more power is asked of the wires than they can carry. Those homes are grey, and the engine counts the quarter hour as unsafe, never as safe.
try.row_failed: Quarter hours with no power-flow solution
try.changes_alone: with the changes but no fix: {value}
try.nosolve: In {n} quarter hours the power flow has no solution: the street is asked to carry more than its wires can, and the voltage collapses. GridTwin counts every one of them as unsafe.
player.night_high: No solar and power flowing from the grid, yet the voltage is high: nothing is generated at night, so there is no reverse flow. The voltage is high because the grid supplies it high, and at night the light demand drops it only a little along the wires.
home.archive_note: For a past day, demand is the month's typical weekday or weekend curve and the grid voltage follows the season and the same date of an earlier year, so days of the same month look alike at night. Only the sunshine is specific to the day. The real tomorrow uses day-ahead forecasts for that date.
